candidates.label: Khirbet Qana
candidates.support: Excavations since the late 1990s found a Jewish village occupied from the Hellenistic through Roman periods, including caves later adapted for Christian pilgrimage veneration with inscriptions invoking Jesus; many recent archaeologists favor this site over Kafr Kanna.

candidates.label: Kafr Kanna
candidates.support: Venerated by pilgrims since at least the medieval period and the traditional site shown to tourists today; the Digital Atlas of the Roman Empire and Pleiades both flag their own identification of this site with ancient Cana as uncertain, and their approximately 2 km-precision points differ from Wikidata's village-center point by about 1.2 km, reflecting genuine positional imprecision rather than a firm alternative location.

candidates.label: Qana
candidates.support: A longstanding minority tradition, especially in Lebanese Christian communities, identifies this southern Lebanese village with biblical Cana; both the Digital Atlas of the Roman Empire and Pleiades catalog the site's own existence at this location as certain, but this reflects certainty about the site, not scholarly consensus that it is the Cana of John 2, which is set within Galilee.

summary.text: Cana of Galilee was a village in Galilee, which in the first century AD was part of Herod Antipas's tetrarchy. The Gospel of John names it as the place of Jesus' first recorded sign, turning water into wine at a wedding, and of a second episode set there; its identification is disputed among several candidate villages, and this map favors none of them.

history.text: John's Gospel sets a wedding feast at Cana, attended by Jesus' mother, where Jesus turned water into wine in six stone water jars kept "after the Jews' way of purifying"; John calls this the beginning of Jesus' signs. John later brings Jesus back to Cana, where a nobleman whose son was sick at Capernaum came to him and begged him to heal his son. One of the disciples, Nathanael, was from Cana.

Excavations at Khirbet Qana, the first candidate, uncovered a Jewish village with caves later adapted for Christian pilgrimage. Kafr Kanna, the second, has been venerated by pilgrims since at least the medieval period and has been the site most visited by pilgrims since the seventeenth century; excavations beneath its Franciscan church found remains of a Jewish building from the third and fourth centuries, perhaps a synagogue, though its first-century archaeological evidence is thinner. A third, minority identification places Cana at Qana in southern Lebanon; John calls the village "Cana of Galilee."

Today at Kafr Kanna a Franciscan church, blessed in 1881, marks the traditional site of the wedding, and a chapel built in 1885 nearby honors Nathanael. Khirbet Qana is an archaeological site with no modern village, about 9 km north-northwest of Kafr Kanna.

scripture.textWEB: The third day, there was a wedding in Cana of Galilee. Jesus’ mother was there.
Now there were six water pots of stone set there after the Jews’ way of purifying, containing two or three metretes apiece.
This beginning of his signs Jesus did in Cana of Galilee, and revealed his glory; and his disciples believed in him.
Jesus came therefore again to Cana of Galilee, where he made the water into wine. There was a certain nobleman whose son was sick at Capernaum.
Simon Peter, Thomas called Didymus, Nathanael of Cana in Galilee, and the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples were together.

Now in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judea, and Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, and his brother Philip tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene,
When he heard that Jesus had come out of Judea into Galilee, he went to him and begged him that he would come down and heal his son, for he was at the point of death.

politicalHistory.entity: Kingdom of Herod the Great (ruler: Herod the Great)
Tetrarchy of Galilee and Perea (ruler: Herod Antipas)
Kingdom of Herod Agrippa I (ruler: Herod Agrippa I)

politicalHistory.note: Nero later added the Galilean towns of Tiberias and Tarichaeae (identified with Magdala), and Julias in Perea with fourteen villages, to Agrippa II's kingdom; Josephus dates this to AD 54, but the Jewish Encyclopedia reads Agrippa II's coinage as pointing to AD 61 instead. These are towns, not land of their own, so this area's extent does not change.
